title: Cold→Hot transition: quick scratchpad and benchmark log
body:
Purpose:
Quick, messy notes from a few small-scale runs exploring how the serving runtime transitions from cold (no KV/prefill) to hot (primed KV cache + warmed kernels). Goal: capture numbers, rough graphs, and next actions. Not a formal runbook—just me journaling results to iterate on hypotheses.

Hypotheses I wanted to test:
- H1: A small, targeted priming (first N requests with short context) buys >30% reduction in p95 for subsequent longer-context requests.
- H2: Continuous low-rate background priming (1 req / 5s) is cheaper than bulk priming bursts for the same steady-state p95.
- H3: Switching to qkv-cache-aware kernels gives diminishing returns once KV hit-rate > 85%.

Environment / Setup (notes):
- Cluster: dev-dedicated-pool-3 (4x A100.80GB-equivalent), single model per node.
- Model binary: openlm-13b-q4_0 (quantized, KV-cache enabled).
- Serving runtime: local branch feature/kernel-opt-jan26 (PR#1425) with adaptive-kernel-selection turned on.
- Traffic generator: bench/playback.py (simple poisson/gamma arrival modes) with client that can set arrival distribution and attach "priming" requests.
- Test payload: prompt length 64 tokens + completion target 128 tokens (avg generated tokens ~110).
- Measurement: token-level timing + request-level latencies. Report p50/p95/p99 (ms) and throughput (tokens/s).

Run matrix (short):
- A: Cold baseline (no priming), Poisson arrival, target QPS 20, 50, 100. 10 min runs.
- B: Bulk priming: send 100 priming requests (short context) then run A traffic.
- C: Background priming: 1 priming req / 5s during A traffic.
- D: Kernel toggle: same as B but disable kernel-optimizations to compare.

Selected commands (for my future self):
- priming seq: python bench/playback.py --mode priming --count 100 --prompt-template short_prime.txt --target-model /models/openlm-13b-q4_0
- run load: python bench/playback.py --mode poisson --qps 50 --duration 600 --arrival-shape 1.2 --target-model ...
- fetch traces: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://console.internal/api/traces?run=2025-09-18-coldhot-1 > run-trace.json

Raw highlights (picked from aggregated CSVs):
- Cold baseline, QPS=50: p50=210ms, p95=880ms, p99=1.6s, tokens/s=5200
- After bulk priming (100 short primes), QPS=50: p50=190ms, p95=470ms, p99=820ms, tokens/s=5400
- Background priming (1/5s), QPS=50: p50=195ms, p95=520ms, p99=950ms, tokens/s=5350
- Kernel-disabled (same priming as bulk), QPS=50: p50=205ms, p95=720ms, p99=1.2s, tokens/s=5250

Interpretation / quick thoughts:
- Bulk priming moved p95 ~45% down vs cold baseline for this workload (64+128). That's consistent with the hypothesis that initial KV fill matters for p95.
- Background priming also helps but not as much as a concentrated priming burst for the same CPU/GPU cycles (we expended ~100 priming requests in bulk vs ~120 priming requests over 10 minutes in background; bulk wins for immediate p95 improvement).
- Kernel opt toggle shows the runtime optimizations still matter: priming + optimized kernels gives the best p95; removing kernel opt drags p95 back up significantly. So both kernel choice and cache hit-rate interact.

Small ASCII "chart" (p95 vs QPS, sketch):
- QPS 20  : cold 240ms | primed 120ms
- QPS 50  : cold 880ms | primed 470ms
- QPS 100 : cold 1.4s | primed 980ms
(so effectiveness drops at higher QPS—likely contention/queuing + batching effects)

Cost shorthand (rough):
- Bulk priming cost: +~0.7% GPU tokens for the burst, but reduced tail latency for ~15 minutes. If priming can be amortized across user sessions it's a good trade.
- Background priming cost: continuous small overhead (~0.1% tokens/s sustained) but less p95 improvement per token.

Open questions / next quick experiments:
- Q1: Is there an optimal priming vector (mix of short vs medium-length primes) that hits an inflection point where background priming becomes as effective as bulk? Plan: A/B with 50x short primes vs 25x medium primes (256 tokens).
- Q2: Does priming benefit persist across model switch (e.g., fallback to smaller model)? I noticed some contamination of cache entries when switching variants. Potential follow-up: test strict model pinning + priming.
- Q3: How does multi-tenant noise affect this? All runs were single-tenant; multi-tenant will increase eviction rate. Run a two-tenant replay with noisy traffic at 30% capacity.
- Q4: Explore cheaper priming: synthetic embeddings-only priming (no generation) to warm KV entries with fewer token costs.

Notes-to-self / debugging observations:
- Saw occasional outliers (one-off 6s p99) correlated with GC spike on node (python worker). Add GC metrics to next run logs.
- When dumping traces, noticed priming requests had higher variance in kernel selection on the first minute; the adaptive-kernel-selection code needs a more conservative cooldown to avoid flip-flopping under bursty priming.
- Trace sample: request_id=rt-20250918-0312 was cold path, kernel v2, kernel-init 42ms, kv-populate 110ms. After priming, similar request had kv-hit 0.94 and kernel switch avoided.

Immediate next actions (short checklist):
- [ ] Re-run A/B with medium-length primes (256 tokens) and measure hit-rate vs token cost.
- [ ] Add GC and kernel-switch counters to bench playback output (low priority but useful).
- [ ] Open small GitHub experiment PR that gates priming bursts behind a flag + telemetry (link is PR#1425 but will add new commits).
- [ ] Schedule a quick pairing w/ Ravi to test multi-tenant noisy-run (we both free Friday 11am).

Wrap-up/one-liner summary:
Bulk priming (one-time, small burst) gives the biggest immediate p95 reduction for long-context generations; background priming is cheaper but less effective per token. Kernel optimization multiplies the benefit. Need multi-tenant and cost-amortization experiments to make a product recommendation.
